We should never forget that the two most divisive and destructive American
presidents in living memory, George W. Bush and Donald J. Trump, were elected
to their first terms after losing the popular vote; after winning _fewer_
votes than their Democratic opponents. Al Gore beat Bush in 2000 by half a
million votes. Hillary Clinton trumped Trump in 2016 by a whopping 3 million
votes. Yet, thanks to this country's archaic and anti-democratic Electoral
College, Bush and Trump joined [three other American
presidents](https://www.nationalpopularvote.com/5-47-presidents-came-office-
without-winning-national-popular-vote) in winning the White House despite
losing the popular vote.

The Electoral College, which grants the presidency to the candidate who
receives a simple majority of at least 270 of 538 total electoral votes, comes
from [Article II, Section 1, Clauses 2 and
3](https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/article-2/section-1/). It was a
consequence of delegates to the 1787 Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia
[fearing](https://www.history.com/articles/electoral-college-founding-fathers-
constitutional-convention) a direct democracy and the rise of populist
demagogues (oh, the irony!).

Americans, however, aren't fans of the Electoral College - and not just
because of the Bush and Trump victories. [Opinion
polls](https://news.gallup.com/vault/192704/gallup-vault-rejecting-electoral-
college.aspx) dating back to the 1940s show clear majorities in favor of
switching to a national popular vote. Yet the Electoral College persists
because the constitutional amendment needed to abolish it is a near-
impossibility.

So what can be done? Well, intriguingly, _tantalizingly_ , here's how the
Democratic Party's blue tsunami in last week's midterms could perhaps finish
off the Electoral College for good.
